recorded.text: Even when the storm rages, his presence ensures you're never truly alone.
For anyone who knows Jesus but still feels the panic rising. Let's slow down and give Scripture our attention.

recorded.prompt: library:peace-3.mp3

recorded.text:
Here's something to sit with.

When fear takes over, what would change if you remembered he's still in the boat with you?

Bring your fear to Jesus right now and ask him to calm what feels out of control.
Even true disciples can be overwhelmed by fear when the storm is real enough.
Even Peter, James, and John cried out 'Master, we're going to perish!'
When the storm had passed, Jesus asked them, 'Where is your faith?'
That's the question.
Having true saving faith is one thing.
Having that faith ready for use when something unexpected happens is another.
Many people receive Christ as their Savior and commit their souls to him for time and eternity, yet their faith fails them when they're suddenly tried.
The faith that carries you through a storm is the faith that sees him who is invisible.
It finds Jesus near you in the darkest hour, and blue sky behind the blackest cloud.
The disciples had Jesus right there in the boat with them, yet when the water started coming in they were sure they were going to die.
They forgot his care for them.
They forgot that as long as they were with him they had to be safe, whatever happened.
Sight and sense and feeling make us poor theologians.
That's humbling, but it's also instructive.
It teaches us what to watch for in our own hearts, and what to expect in other believers.
We have to be moderate in our expectations.
A person can have real faith and still show great weakness sometimes.

Here's where we're reading today. Luke 8:24. They came to him, and awoke him, saying, “Master, master, we are dying!” He awoke, and rebuked the wind and the raging of the water, and they ceased, and it was calm. Let's watch.
True compassion moves beyond words to tangible acts of love.
Why did the religious men walk past someone dying? Let's slow down together before the day takes over.

recorded.prompt: library:hope-5.mp3

recorded.text:
Here's something to sit with.

Where is God calling you to stop and help when it would be easier to keep walking?

Ask God to show you one person today who needs the kind of love that costs you something.
True brotherly love is rare.
Selfishness is the leading trait of most people.
That cheap charity which costs nothing more than a small donation is common enough.
But that self-sacrificing kindness which doesn't care what trouble it takes, as long as good can be done, is a grace rarely met with.
The only person who helped the wounded traveler was a Samaritan, a man from a nation that had no dealings with the Jews.
He saw a man stripped and lying half dead.
He asked no questions but at once had compassion.
He made no excuses but at once gave aid.
And Jesus says to us, 'Go and do likewise.' The Samaritan's compassion wasn't confined to feelings.
He took real trouble to give help.
He acted as well as felt.
Jesus tells us about a man beaten by thieves and left half dead on the road.
He went to him, bound up his wounds, set him on his own donkey, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.

The next day he gave the innkeeper money, saying, 'Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I'll repay you when I come back.' The kindness of a Christian toward others should not be in word only but in deed and in truth.
It should be a practical love, a love which costs something in money and time and trouble.
A priest came by and saw him.
Then a Levite came by and saw him.
Both were religious men who should have been ready to help someone in distress.
But both were too selfish or too unfeeling to offer any help.

They probably told themselves they didn't know this man, that he'd maybe gotten into trouble through his own fault, that they had no time to stop, that they had enough to do minding their own business without troubling themselves with strangers.
So one after the other, they both passed by on the other side.
This is an exact picture of what goes on constantly in the world.
Here's where we're reading today. Luke 10:37. He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.” Let's watch.
Grace finds you right where your hunger leads you.
For anyone who feels too compromised to approach Jesus boldly. Today is also World Humanitarian Day. Let's slow down and give Scripture our attention.

recorded.prompt: library:hope-1.mp3

recorded.text:
Here's something to sit with.

What part of your past are you still letting whisper that you don't belong in his presence?

Ask Jesus to show you one place where shame is keeping you at a distance, and let him call you by name today.
Zacchaeus was the chief of the publicans, the head tax collector, a man with real authority and a considerable estate.
Just because many tax collectors were corrupt didn't mean all of them were.
Just because Zacchaeus had lived badly in the past didn't mean his heart was still the same now.
And even if he was still a sinner, that was exactly why Christ came to him.
A physician goes to the sick, not to the healthy.
Christ was in no danger of being corrupted by Zacchaeus.
He was there to do good, and Zacchaeus received him joyfully.
That day, salvation came to his house.
What looks scandalous to a narrow soul is often grace doing exactly what it came to do.
When Jesus came through Jericho, this wealthy, powerful man forgot his dignity entirely.
He ran ahead through the crowd like a boy and climbed a tree just to catch a glimpse of Jesus.
That eagerness mattered.
When Jesus reached the spot, he looked up, saw him, and called him by name: 'Zacchaeus, hurry and come down.
Today I must stay at your house.' Grace met him right where his hunger had brought him.
The crowd murmured immediately.
They saw Zacchaeus as a sinner, someone Christ had no business associating with.
But their judgment was unfair on every count.

Here's where we're reading today. Luke 19:5. When Jesus came to the place, he looked up and saw him, and said to him, “Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must stay at your house.” Let's watch.
Grace that finds you is grace that will not leave you the same.
Jesus stopped for the man everyone despised. Let's give this a few unhurried minutes.

recorded.text:
Here's something to sit with.

Is there a place in your life where his grace has been received, but hasn't shown itself yet?

Ask God to show you where his grace is asking for more than words from you.
Jesus came to seek and save the lost, and no one is too far gone for his grace.
When a wealthy person begins to give away his riches and someone who cheated others starts making restitution, you know something has changed.
Old things have passed away, and all things become new.
Freely pardoned and raised from death to life, Zacchaeus felt he couldn't wait to show whose he was.
A faith that doesn't purify your heart and life isn't saving faith at all.
The heart that has truly tasted Christ's grace will instinctively hate sin and want to live differently.
That's the evidence that matters.
Look at Zacchaeus.
Jesus stopped and spoke to him without being asked.
He invited himself to the house of a tax collector, and that very day he sent his renewing grace into Zacchaeus's heart and made him a child of God.
If ever there was a soul sought and saved without having done anything to deserve it, it was Zacchaeus.
That's the shape his grace takes: it moves first, before we're worthy of it, before we've done anything to earn it.
When Zacchaeus met Jesus, something real happened.
He promised to give half his possessions to the poor and repay anyone he'd cheated four times over.
That's not just words.
Here's where we're reading today. Luke 19:10. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost.” Let's watch.
